stem: At operation for complex congenital heart disease, the surgeon inspects an opened atrium. Which finding identifies it as the **morphologic right atrium**?

choices.text: The flap valve of the fossa ovalis (septum primum) forming its septal surface
A limbus surrounding the valve of the fossa ovalis superiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly
A long, narrow appendage with a windsock appearance
The orifices of the four pulmonary veins entering the chamber
Its rightward spatial position in the chest

explanation.text: The **limbus of the fossa ovalis** is on the ==right atrial== septal surface; the left atrial septal surface shows the **flap valve** (septum primum) instead.

head: Feature
Right atrium
Left atrium
rows: **Flap valve** of the fossa ovalis (septum primum)
None at the base of the appendage
explanation.caption: Telling the atria apart

explanation.text: The limbus is **C-shaped**: it surrounds the fossa ovalis (in the center of the atrial septum) on its **superior, anterior, and posterior** aspects.

explanation.title: Position is not identity
explanation.text: Chambers are identified **by their morphology, regardless of their spatial positions**. A rightward atrium is not necessarily a morphologic right atrium.

Morphologic characteristics important for identifying the right atrium are presence of the limbus of the fossa ovalis, which surrounds the valve of the fossa ovalis (septum primum) superiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly

choiceNotes.a: The flap valve of the fossa ovalis (septum primum) characterizes the **left** atrial septal surface.
choiceNotes.c: A long, narrow, windsock appendage is the best indicator of a **left** atrium.
choiceNotes.d: The left atrium normally receives the pulmonary venous drainage from the **four pulmonary veins**.
choiceNotes.e: Chambers are identified by their **morphology, regardless of their spatial positions**.

stem: In the opened right atrium, which structure separates the **trabeculated** portion from the smooth (venous) portion?

choices.text: Tendon of Todaro
Limbus of the fossa ovalis
Eustachian valve
Crista terminalis
Thebesian valve

explanation.text: The **crista terminalis** (the inside of the sulcus terminalis) separates the ==trabeculated== from the ==nontrabeculated (venous)== portions of the right atrium.

children: a boundary of the triangle of Koch

explanation.title: Left atrium
explanation.text: There is **no crista terminalis** at the base of the left atrial appendage.
crista terminalis, which separates trabeculated from nontrabeculated (venous) portions of the atrium

choiceNotes.a: The tendon of Todaro is a boundary of the **triangle of Koch**, with the coronary sinus and the septal tricuspid leaflet anulus.
choiceNotes.b: The limbus surrounds the **fossa ovalis** superiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly.
choiceNotes.c: The eustachian valve lies at the **orifice of the inferior vena cava**.
choiceNotes.e: The thebesian valve lies at the **orifice of the coronary sinus**.

stem: Echocardiography in an infant with **tricuspid atresia** shows prominent membranes that appear to divide the right atrium into two parts. These most likely represent:

choices.text: A hypertrophied crista terminalis
An enlarged limbus of the fossa ovalis
A leftward-juxtaposed right atrial appendage
A prominent tendon of Todaro
Prominent eustachian and thebesian valves

explanation.text: The **eustachian and thebesian valves** may be prominent enough to appear to ==divide the right atrium into two parts==, a common finding in **tricuspid atresia**.

Normal structures are sometimes expressed in an **excessive or unusual manner**. They are not themselves functionally important abnormalities, but they are **usually associated with cardiac malformations**.

head: Unusual expression
Comment
rows: Appear to divide the right atrium; common in **tricuspid atresia**
explanation.caption: Normal structures, unusual expression

explanation.title: A clue, not a lesion
explanation.text: Juxtaposition of the atrial appendages is **usually associated with cardiac malformations**.
Thus, the eustachian and thebesian valves may be sufficiently prominent to appear to divide the right atrium into two parts, a common finding in tricuspid atresia.

choiceNotes.a: The crista terminalis separates the trabeculated from the venous portion; the source does not describe it dividing the atrium in tricuspid atresia.
choiceNotes.b: The limbus surrounds the fossa ovalis on the septum; it is not the structure described as dividing the atrium.
choiceNotes.c: Juxtaposition describes the **position of the appendage**, not membranes dividing the atrium.
choiceNotes.d: The tendon of Todaro is a boundary of the triangle of Koch, not the structure described as dividing the atrium.

stem: In some patients the atria are **not in their normal position**. In such a case, which feature is the **most secure indicator** that an atrium is morphologically a right atrium?

choices.text: A wide-based, blunt-ended atrial appendage
Its rightward position in the chest
A long, narrow, windsock-shaped appendage
Receipt of the pulmonary venous drainage
A flap valve of the fossa ovalis on its septal surface

explanation.text: When the atria are malpositioned, the ==wide-based, blunt-ended right atrial appendage== is the **most secure indicator** of a morphologic right atrium.

head: Right atrial appendage
Left atrial appendage
rows: Most secure indicator of a right atrium
Best indicator of a left atrium
explanation.caption: The appendage identifies the atrium

explanation.text: **Other indicators** of the atria and atrial situs:

items: **Venous drainage**
The situs indicated by the **pulmonary artery** anatomy
The situs indicated by the **bronchial** anatomy

explanation.title: Where it matters most
explanation.text: Morphologic identification of each atrium becomes particularly important in conditions such as **heterotaxy** (Chapter 53).

The atria are not in normal position in some patients; in these cases, the wide-based, blunt-ended right atrial appendage is the most secure indicator that an atrium is morphologically a right atrium.

choiceNotes.b: Chambers are identified by their morphology, **regardless of their spatial positions**.
choiceNotes.c: A long, narrow, windsock appendage is the best indicator of a **left** atrium.
choiceNotes.d: The left atrium is the chamber that normally receives the **pulmonary venous** drainage.
choiceNotes.e: The flap valve (septum primum) characterizes the **left** atrial septal surface; the right side shows the limbus.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the **morphologic left atrium**?

choices.text: Its septal surface shows the limbus of the fossa ovalis
It normally receives the major portion of the coronary venous drainage
Its appendage is the only trabeculated structure within it
A thebesian valve guards one of its venous orifices
It normally receives the inferior and superior venae cavae

explanation.text: The **left atrial appendage** is the ==only trabeculated structure== in the left atrium, and there is **no crista terminalis** at its base.

items: Normally receives **pulmonary venous drainage** from the four pulmonary veins
Septal surface: the **flap valve** of the fossa ovalis (septum primum)
Appendage: **long and narrow**, windsock appearance; the best indicator of a morphologic left atrium
No crista terminalis; the appendage is the only trabeculated structure

explanation.text: In general, the left atrium is located **by exclusion**, after identifying the position of the right atrium.

explanation.title: Right-sided features
explanation.text: The limbus, crista terminalis, eustachian and thebesian valves, venae cavae and coronary sinus all belong to the **right** atrium.
There is no crista terminalis at the base of the left atrial appendage, the only trabeculated structure in the left atrium.

choiceNotes.a: The limbus is on the **right** atrioseptal surface; the left side shows the flap valve (septum primum).
choiceNotes.b: The **right** atrium normally receives the major portion of coronary venous drainage, from the coronary sinus.
choiceNotes.d: The thebesian valve lies at the orifice of the **coronary sinus**, in the right atrium.
choiceNotes.e: The **right** atrium normally receives systemic venous drainage from the venae cavae.

stem: Which part of the heart occupies **most of its anterior aspect**?

Right atrium

Left atrium

stem: Where does the aorta lie relative to the pulmonary trunk at the level of the **pericardial reflection**?

choices.text: Anterior and to the right
Anterior and to the left
Posterior and to the left
Posterior and to the right
Directly anterior

explanation.text: By the pericardial reflection the aorta is ==anterior and to the right== of the pulmonary trunk, although it originates **posterior** and to the right at the base of the heart.

explanation.title: Same vessels, different level
explanation.text: Do not confuse the two levels: the aorta stays to the **right**, but moves from **posterior** (base) to **anterior** (pericardial reflection).
Aorta originates posterior and to the right of the pulmonary trunk at the base of the heart but is anterior and to the right by the pericardial reflection

choiceNotes.b: The aorta lies to the **right** of the pulmonary trunk at both levels described.
choiceNotes.c: The aorta lies to the **right** of the pulmonary trunk at both levels described.
choiceNotes.d: Posterior and to the right is where the aorta **originates, at the base of the heart**, not its position at the pericardial reflection.
choiceNotes.e: At the pericardial reflection the aorta is anterior **and to the right** of the pulmonary trunk.

stem: During **mitral valve replacement**, viewed from the right side as at operation, which area is marked as the area of **greatest risk to the aortic valve**?

choices.text: Right trigone
Base of the left atrial appendage
Anulus of the posterior mitral leaflet
Septum primum
Left trigone

explanation.text: The ==left trigone== is the area of **greatest risk to the aortic valve** during mitral valve replacement.

head: Area (Fig. 1.4)
What is at risk
rows: Area of greatest risk to the **aortic valve** during mitral valve replacement
explanation.caption: Two trigones, two different dangers

explanation.title: Related anatomy
explanation.text: The leftward half of the anterior mitral leaflet is in **fibrous continuity with the aortic valve** (the aortic-mitral anulus).
Crosshatching marks left trigone, the area of greatest risk to aortic valve during mitral valve replacement.

choiceNotes.a: The right trigone **contains the bundle of His**; the left trigone is the area of greatest risk to the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.b: The base of the left atrial appendage is a left atrial landmark in Fig. 1.4, not the area of risk to the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.c: Fig. 1.4 marks the **left trigone**, not the posterior leaflet, as the area of greatest risk to the aortic valve.
choiceNotes.d: The septum primum is the flap valve of the fossa ovalis on the left atrial septal surface.

stem: Which topographic feature identifies a ventricle as the **morphologic left ventricle** rather than the right?

choices.text: Its inlet and outlet valves are widely separated
Its entire sinus portion is coarsely trabeculated
Its inlet and outlet valves lie juxtaposed within its base
A moderator band runs from its septum to its free wall
Small papillary muscles attach to its septal surface

Left ventricle

Much smaller outlet beneath a semilunar valve

the trabeculations are characteristically fine compared with those in the right ventricle.

stem: The outlet portion of the right ventricular septal surface has three components. Which is the **largest**, separating the pulmonary valve from the aortic and tricuspid valves?

choices.text: Anterior (superior) extension of the trabecula septomarginalis
Moderator band
Narrow anterior extension superior to the trabecular septum
Infundibular (conal) septum
Membranous septum

explanation.text: The ==infundibular (conal) septum== is the largest component of the right ventricular outlet septum; it separates the **pulmonary** valve from the **aortic and tricuspid** valves.

items: **Inlet** portion: surrounds and supports the tricuspid valve
**Trabecular** (apical trabecular) portion: the coarse pattern typical of the right ventricle

items.text: **Outlet** portion: smooth but complex, three components
items: **Infundibular (conal) septum**, the largest
Anterior (superior) extension of the **TSM** (septal band)
A small, very anterior extension superior to the trabecular septum

explanation.text: Alternatively, the right ventricular septal surface may be divided into **posterior (basal), middle, apical (anterior), and infundibular (conal)** portions.
The largest is the infundibular (conal) septum, which separates the pulmonary from the aortic and tricuspid valves.

choiceNotes.a: The anterior extension of the TSM is the **second** component of the outlet septum, not the largest.
choiceNotes.b: The moderator band runs from the septum to the free wall, continuous with the TSM apically; it is not an outlet septal component.
choiceNotes.c: This narrow, very anterior portion is the **third, small** component.
choiceNotes.e: The membranous septum is not one of the three components of the outlet portion described.

stem: Why is the most distal, cephalad portion of the infundibular septum **not, strictly speaking, part of the ventricular septum** in the normal heart?

choices.text: It is fibrous tissue continuous with the membranous septum
It is formed by the anterior (superior) extension of the trabecula septomarginalis
It forms the muscular portion of the atrioventricular septum
It is separated from the septum by the ventriculoinfundibular fold
The pulmonary valve arises from a cone of muscle, without septal attachment

explanation.text: In the normal heart the **pulmonary valve arises from the apex of a ==cone of muscle==** and has **no septal attachment**, so the most cephalad infundibular septum is not truly ventricular septum.

items: Only **part** of the infundibular septum is interventricular (Fig. 1.5: its rightward portion and the inferior part of its central portion).
In some malformations, e.g. **double outlet right ventricle**, **none** of it may be interventricular.

explanation.title: Infundibular septum ≠ interventricular septum

the pulmonary valve arises from the apex of a cone of muscle and does not have a septal attachment.

choiceNotes.a: The infundibular septum is **muscle**; the reason given is the pulmonary valve's origin from a cone of muscle.
choiceNotes.b: The anterior (superior) extension of the **TSM** is a **separate** component of the outlet septum; the reason given is the pulmonary valve’s origin from a cone of muscle.
choiceNotes.c: In Fig. 1.13 the **AV septum** is the septal tissue above the line of attachment of the tricuspid septal leaflet, not the cephalad end of the infundibular septum.
choiceNotes.d: The **ventriculoinfundibular fold** is part of the right ventricular free wall, partially overlain by the parietal band; it is not the reason given.

stem: According to the right ventricular anatomy described in the chapter, where do **ventricular septal defects most commonly occur**?

choices.text: Within the coarsely trabeculated apical portion of the sinus septum
Within the inlet septum beneath the septal tricuspid leaflet
At the junction of the anterosuperior outlet and posteroinferior sinus portions
Within the most distal cephalad portion of the infundibular septum
At the attachment of the moderator band to the free wall

explanation.text: VSDs most commonly occur at the ==junction of the outlet and sinus portions== of the right ventricle, hence the names **“junctional”** or **“conoventricular”**.
The outlet–sinus junction is clearly demarcated **only along the lower margin of the outlet portion of the septum**.
It is in this area that ventricular septal defects (VSDs) most commonly occur; the morphology of the area gives the name “junctional” or “conoventricular” to these defects.

choiceNotes.a: The source names the **outlet–sinus junction**, not the apical trabecular septum, as the most common site.
choiceNotes.b: The source names the **outlet–sinus junction**, not the inlet septum, as the most common site.
choiceNotes.d: The most cephalad infundibular septum is not strictly ventricular septum at all; VSDs are most common at the outlet–sinus junction.
choiceNotes.e: The moderator band is only one part of the ridge; VSDs occur in the septal area of the outlet–sinus junction.

stem: In the normal left ventricle, which part of the mitral valve is in **fibrous continuity with the aortic valve** (the aortic-mitral anulus)?

explanation.text: The ==leftward half of the anterior mitral leaflet== is in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve: the **aortic-mitral anulus**.

stem: In the normal heart, which **right ventricular** structure lies **opposite the aortic valve** and may occasionally be displaced into the left ventricular outflow beneath it?
